IntroductionThis paper is the first in a two-part series that outlines the origins of LayerZero, the cross-chain messaging protocol now connecting most of the multi-chain world, and its impending launch of Zero, an effort to rebuild the Layer 1 stack from first principles. Part One focuses on LayerZero: the way in which the team built the protocol, the structural limits of today's blockchain architectures based on lessons learned from five years of deep integration with 170+ chains, and the team’s motivation to design an entirely new base layer. Part Two will introduce that base layer—Zero—including its architectural substrate, the bottlenecks it addresses, and why we think it represents a breakthrough for blockchain infrastructure.In this series, we aim to present a holistic view of LayerZero's existing business, including lessons learned and the design choices that should help Zero redefine the base layer. In our view, investors must understand these dynamics to understand LayerZero’s trajectory and gauge Zero’s potential for success.Framing And ThesisBlockchains are programmable ledgers: hermetic and isolated ecosystems impervious to outside data and/or parties, and designed to guarantee security and immutability. Ethereum does not know what is happening on Solana. Solana does not know what is happening on Arbitrum. Each chain is its own sovereign ledger, with its own consensus mechanism, its own finality model, and its own state. They share nothing.With only one relevant chain, the hermetic seal was not a problem. From its launch in 2015 through 2021, Ethereum was the only programmable ledger of consequence: all assets and contracts operated within the same ecosystem. Thereafter, its hermetic seal became a problem when applications, users, and liquidity fragmented across dozens of emerging chains, each launched for different reasons and with different tradeoffs.Consider a simple, hypothetical institutional example. A portfolio manager holds $20 million in a tokenized money market fund on Ethereum—a net asset value (NAV)-stable, Treasury-backed instrument earning 4.8% annually. A lending protocol on Solana accepts that token as collateral, allowing the manager to borrow SOL and deploy it into a higher-yielding Solana-native strategy, all without redeeming the underlying position. The economics might seem straightforward, but the execution is not.For most of crypto's history, natively moving assets between and among chains was not possible. A token on Ethereum stayed on Ethereum. If a higher yielding opportunity existed elsewhere, a holder would have to sell ether and reinvest on another chain, paying fees and taxes and taking time, while incurring another layer of risk in the process. Because tokens could not interact with contracts on other chains, applications gravitated toward liquidity instead. Aave and Uniswap, for example, see the majority of their activity consolidated among a few chains but have still deployed instances across dozens of chains, despite each reflecting the same code, application, and use cases.Highlighting the structural problem is the scale of the current workaround economy. Year-to-date, across all bridging and messaging mechanisms, cross-chain value transfers have totaled $580 billion and are on track to clear $1+ trillion for the year.1 For perspective, cross chain transfers this year are 4x the size of all prediction markets and have cumulated to more than half of all DEX (decentralized exchange) spot volume. By volume, cross-chain transfers now rank among the largest primitives2 in all of crypto, exceeded only by perps3 and spot trading.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from DefiLlama as of June 11, 2026. For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security or cryptocurrency. Past performance is not indicative of future results.LayerZero set out to rebuild this primitive with a mechanism enabling chains to exchange verified truth without a custodian. Its deeper ambition is to enable the omnichain transfer of any logic or information, not just tokens—for example, a governance vote on Ethereum that executes on Arbitrum, a collateral position on Solana that triggers a liquidation on Base, or a compliance check that follows an asset wherever it moves.The Fragmentation ProblemLayer Zero’s raison d’etre evolved because of the fragmentation into hundreds of blockchains. For years, Ethereum accounted for almost all programmable activity. Then, three forces caused an explosion in fragmentation. Understanding those three forces is key to finding a solution to the problem.Technical Necessity. Physically, Ethereum could not host the overwhelming demand it attracted. As measured by throughput and bandwidth caps, the EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) was at full capacity constantly, so much so that blockspace pricing soared and punished every application hosted on the network. Ethereum's answer was not to scale the base layer but to "launch more chains," in what is known today as the rollup-centric roadmap.Capital Incentives. Starting with Ethereum’s launch in 2017, investors have paid enormous premiums for teams that launched their own chains, especially EVM-compatible ones. New Layer 1s (L1s) L1s or Layer 2s (L2s)4 with tokens were worth multiples of the same applications deployed on other chains. The monetization model rewarded chain proliferation, so chains proliferated.Architectural Specialization. Some applications did and do require base-layer customization. A derivatives DEX optimizing a matching engine, for example, cannot share a fee market with non-fungible token (NFT) mints or meme coin launches. Hyperliquid is an important case in point.As a result, hundreds of active blockchains proliferated, each with its own consensus mechanism, execution environment, and security assumptions. While the market today is subject to power-law dynamics, a nontrivial amount of capital still resides in the long tail as different chains are optimizing for different goals. The largest four are Bitcoin for settlement, Ethereum for programmability, Solana for throughput, Hyperliquid for perpetuals.To separate signal from noise, we have compiled most Layer 1, Layer 2, and app-chains, screened for total value locked (TVL) above $20 million or market capitalization above $50 million, as shown below.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from CoinGecko, DefiLlama, and CoinMarketCap as of June 11, 2026. For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security or cryptocurrency.Charting all three forces, ~150 chains cleared those thresholds. Layer 1 launches—such as Avalanche and Solana—dominated through 2020. Then, led by Arbitrum and Optimism, Layer 2s arrived in force when Ethereum formalized its rollup roadmap. Finally, app-chains like Hyperliquid and dYdX chain increased as a share of launches into 2023 and 2024.The resulting fragmentation created a structural problem with significant consequences. Liquidity splintered across chains, the same asset trading at different depths with different counterparties under different settlement assumptions. An asset that existed on only one chain was and is functionally less useful, its addressable market capped by the participants in that ecosystem. Moreover, every cross-chain movement compounded the settlement risk, every hop introducing a new set of trust assumptions, a different security threshold, and a new timeframe for assets in transit and at rest.The industry's first answer was to sell on one chain and buy on another—akin to moving the stock of Coinbase from Schwab to Robinhood. In traditional markets, the in-kind transfer (ACATS) takes roughly a week, so most investors sell on one venue and buy on another, hit by taxes and the spread. Crypto's early years worked similarly, lacking the equivalent of an in-kind asset transfer between blockchains.Layer 2s launched the second generation. In 2020, when Ethereum formalized its rollup-centric roadmap, canonical bridges surfaced: "official" bridges to each L2 connected by the team to its parent chain. The process was straightforward. Deposit a token into a bridge contract that locks on Ethereum and mints a wrapped representation on a destination chain. Burning the wrapped token unlocks the original.The limitations to this strategy were structural. Canonical bridges were chain-specific by design: every L2 team built its own with no direct path between L2s, forcing every transaction to route back through Ethereum. For most rollups, an optimistic5 proof mechanism is used, meaning that the waiting period to withdrawal to Ethereum was seven days, making time-sensitive transactions impossible for capital allocation decisions. Every bridge produced its own wrapped version of the token, the lack of interoperability between wrappers fragmenting liquidity further. Complicating matters further, a multisig—a small set of private keys held by the team or designated operators—controlled the locked assets and had to protect them from hacks, coercion, or compromise.In answer to canonical bridges that were too slow and siloed, third-party bridge protocols independent from chains evolved. Instead of routing through Ethereum, they connected chains directly—Ethereum to Solana, Arbitrum to Avalanche—cutting settlement times from seven days to minutes. Through the same lock-mint-burn model, an independent validator handled the verification through a permissioned group of nodes that monitored the source chain and then, upon reaching consensus about a deposit, authorized the mint. Wormhole used a 19-node Guardian network, and Multichain a distributed key generation scheme for its operators.In practice, bridges with custody of enormous pools of assets became the highest-value attack surfaces in crypto: Ronin lost $625 million to compromised validator keys,6 Wormhole $325 million to a signature verification bug,7 and Multichain more than $130 million when its operator keys were compromised and lost, sending its CEO to jail.8 Across every major failure, the pattern was the same—custodial design that concentrated the risk. Bridges relied on a small multisig or a permissioned validator set that applications had no ability to inspect, configure, or replace. When compromised through a key leak, a contract bug, or simple collusion, the entire bridge fell apart, and every application with it.Bridges were the first attempt but not the solution to the fragmentation problem. Enter LayerZero. First, the primitive had to change. The problem was not only moving assets but also passing verified truth between chains. Perhaps a generalized messaging primitive would make bridges just one application among many. Moreover, no single security model could serve every use case; so, instead of imposing a security layer on every use case, perhaps verification could be configured for the specific requirements of each application.LayerZeroLayerZero's core design evolved because its team not only understood the reasons for bridge failures but also believed that its infrastructure should communicate verified messages—not assets—between chains. A messaging-centric design would involve a smaller attack surface and a clear trust model without a honeypot in the form of pooled assets at the protocol layer. Liquidity would live at the application layer, owned and managed by applications themselves. LayerZero’s discovery was correct. Thanks to that structural shift, a wide range of cross-chain services has adopted LayerZero’s model.The familiar analogy is TCP/IP, which defined the way packets move between any two computers on the internet, regardless of operating system or application. LayerZero plays the same role for blockchains, defining the way that messages move between any two chains, regardless of consensus mechanism, virtual machine, or execution environment. Every message involves three parties: a sender on the source chain, a receiver on the destination chain, and a verification path between them. LayerZero calls that verification path a “Decentralized Verifier Network,” or “DVN.”DVNs invert the security model of prior cross-chain systems. The protocol does not dictate who verifies messages: each application chooses its own verifier set—internal teams, external operators, or a combination of both. Ondo, Paxos, and USDT0 all operate their own DVNs to secure the cross-chain movement of their tokens. Differentiated from other systems, the application layer determines LayerZero’s security configuration. In systems like Wormhole and Chainlink CCIP, applications share a security model which means that the compromise of their verification layers impacts everything built upon them.LayerZero’s other foundation is the “Endpoint,” an immutable smart contract deployed on every chain it supports to serve as the access point through which applications send and receive verified messages.Two independent layers of security govern this architecture:Intrinsic Security: LayerZero has hard-coded the protocol-level guarantees into the immutable Endpoint contracts, which no one—including LayerZero Labs—can change. This layer ensures censorship resistance and protection against attacks at access points on both chains.Extrinsic Security: Each application tunes the verifier configuration: how many DVNs must sign, who operates them, what thresholds apply? These choices can be updated as verification methods evolve or as an application's value-at-risk increases.For each application built on top of LayerZero, the messaging protocol is only as secure as the configuration of the verifier set. In April 2026, rsETH tested the protocol at scale. Operating under a single-verifier configuration (1-of-1 DVN) that did not match the value-at-risk, the verifier fell victim to a malicious message that enabled a bad actor to receive tokens that should not have been released. The exploit was not a failure of the messaging primitive but a failure to adhere to the configuration required. LayerZero’s response has been to encourage applications building on its protocol to move toward decentralized, multi-verifier setups with a minimum of 3-of-3 DVNs as the default, a standard the protocol should have mandated from the beginning.Importantly, rsETH did not break LayerZero’s architecture: no other messages were forged, and the remedy was not a redesign but a configuration change. In contrast, during the “bridge era,” the same class of failure required a redesign. rsETH also surfaced a subtler lesson about correlated exposure: configuration-level isolation matters more than it appears when many applications converge on the same default verifier. As a result, defaults must be set as if every application were a $100+ million target. And now, each is.To clarify what LayerZero is not:It is not a bridge. Bridges hold liquidity and execute swaps. LayerZero moves messages.It is not custodial. The protocol never takes possession of user assets.It is not a validator network. LayerZero does not run consensus: it inherits the security of the chains it connects.It is not upgradable. Endpoints are immutable: even LayerZero Labs cannot force a security change on an application.It is not a chain. LayerZero is a pure protocol, living in smart contracts on every chain it touches.It is not the arbiter of application security. Each application, not the protocol, configures its verifier set. The Killer Products: OFT & StargateThe most widely adopted product built on LayerZero’s design is Omnichain Fungible Token, or OFT. An OFT exists natively on any chain, a single unified supply sustained through burn-and-mint at the token contract level. When a token moves from Ethereum to Solana, supply on Ethereum is burned and supply on Solana is minted in the same accounting, with no wrapped intermediary and no liquidity pool in between.For tokens that cannot be modified, LayerZero offers the OFT Adapter. At the token's home chain, the adapter locks the original tokens on a chain with existing deployments. Every other chain without existing deployments receives native OFT supply minted against the locked balance. Burning the OFT supply unlocks tokens from the lockbox. The lock-and-unlock mechanism moves tokens between two chains in which both have existing deployments.Because the Adapter is a configurable extension of the OFT standard, a single deployment can combine the two, applying lock/unlock or mint/burn on each chain. The difference between the two is whether the token is new (Native OFT) or deployed (OFT Adapter), as shown below.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from LayerZero Docs and LayerZero Scan as of June 22, 2026.9 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security or cryptocurrency.Institutionally, if a tokenized money market fund (MMF) were to be issued as an OFT, the process would be much less complicated. Because the fund shares exist as a single unified asset across Ethereum and Solana, moving them would burn supply on the source chain and mint it on the destination with one verified LayerZero message: no custody handoff, no separate trusts, no opaque validator set or multisig in the middle. Moreover, LayerZero's composability primitive, lzCompose, would compress the process further: the deposit into and the borrow from the Solana lending protocol can be bundled into the same message flow. Comparing the three flows—third party bridge, non-composable OFT, and composable OFT (lzCompose)—the contrast becomes clear:Third-Party Bridge. Hold the tokenized MMF on Ethereum → bridge to Solana by locking on Ethereum and receiving the wrapped representation → post the wrapped token as collateral → borrow SOL. Third party bridges require three trust assumptions, a custody handoff, and multiple fees. Worse, the collateral held by the lending protocol is a wrapped IOU of the fund token, not the fund token itself. Its value depends on the solvency of the bridge. Moreover, the manager earns the collateral’s yield only if the wrapper passes along the yield, which most do not.Non-Composable OFT. Hold the OFT-enabled MMF on Ethereum → send to Solana via OFT by burning and minting → post the native fund token as collateral → borrow SOL. The bridge disappears. The collateral on Solana is the fund share itself: same issuer, same NAV accrual, same Treasury backing. That said, the manager must sign for multiple transactions and sit unhedged between the mint and the collateral deposit.Composable OFT (lzCompose). Hold the OFT-enabled MMF on Ethereum → sign once. The burn, the mint, the collateral deposit, and the borrow execute as a single composed message flow. The manager goes from idle fund shares on Ethereum to a levered Solana-native position in one signature, never entering an unproductive intermediate state.OFT—both with and without lzCompose—is becoming the industry standard for cross-chain token issuance. More than 100 protocols have built upon it, and it has powered ~600 token deployments.10 OFT’s share of the volume processed by cross-chain token standards has remained dominant since 2024, as shown below, and has consistently fluctuated between 80% and 90% of the market share.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Allium as of June 30, 2026. For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security or cryptocurrency.OFT and Stargate serve different needs on the same messaging layer. Where OFT enables tokens to exist natively across chains as a single unified supply, Stargate is the liquidity venue for non-OFT tokens. Stargate functions like a bridge in terms of flow—deposit assets on one chain, receive them on another—but the trust model is quite different: its unified liquidity pools hold assets at the application layer in transparent on-chain contracts secured by LayerZero messaging, rather than in a  permissioned validator set holding keys. Designed for a division of labor, the protocol moves messages and custodies nothing. Applications that need liquidity own it themselves, and transparently so. Stargate lets users swap and route non-OFT assets across chains without wrapped representations or trusted intermediaries.LayerZero incubated Stargate and, in 2022, spun it out as a DAO (Distributed Autonomous Organization) to operate independently. As it matured into one of the largest cross-chain liquidity venues in the market, the strategic logic of reuniting it with the protocol became clear. In 2025, LayerZero acquired Stargate from the DAO for ~$110 million in an all-token deal which 95% of voting token holders approved, despite a higher all-cash counterbid from Wormhole.11 Choosing the incumbent's lower-priced offer spoke volumes about ecosystem alignment. Taking direct control of its most significant application, LayerZero had a flagship product to anchor its institutional push.With the adoption of both OFT and Stargate, LayerZero has become the dominant player in cross-chain infrastructure. As of June 2026, several statistics12 illustrate its dominance:$280 billion in cumulative value transferred across LayerZero infrastructure.$15+ billion in volume processed through Stargate in 2025.Processed 44% of cross-chain volume in the first half of 2026 across all LayerZero products—Circle’s CCTP did the second most at 41%.~$100 billion in transfers via USDT0, the largest OFT Adapter deployment.1+ million messages processed per month across 66,000+ deployed contracts.170+ supported blockchains.Several issuers, including Tether, Ethena, and PayPal's PYUSD, the last one issued by Paxos.Several institutional DVN operators including Google Cloud, Fidelity Center of Applied Technology, Worldpay, and Deutche Telekom.Results Of LayerZero’s Integration Work During The Past Five YearsTo deploy a LayerZero Endpoint on a new chain, the team had to operate at the lowest levels of that chain's stack, in its bytecode, opcodes, consensus quirks, finality model, and gas semantics. It had to rewrite its Endpoint from scratch to match each chain’s specific characteristics, which was not optional. The Endpoint is the immutable access point through which all the protocol's security guarantees flow.To support 170+ chains, LayerZero had to deconstruct 170+ architectures across the EVM, MoveVM, Solana Virtual Machine (SVM), Cosmos chains, Bitcoin sidechains, and a long tail of other chains. Each chain houses a distinct architecture that determines how computation is scheduled, how state persists, how blocks propagate, and how finality is determined. In that process, the team discovered that surface-level similarities between and among chains camouflaged deep architectural differences. For some chains, LayerZero had to invent new primitives to recognize the differences, creating lzCompose along the way. The MoveVM, for example, did not support the contract interactions standard on EVM natively, forcing the team to design a mechanism for one cross-chain message to trigger multiple layers of logic across both environments without a second signature.Few teams understand the architecture of more than 170 blockchains at that depth, a vantage point that caused an uncomfortable conclusion: interoperability alone is not enough. Messaging can connect fragmented networks but cannot emulate all environments to offer shared liquidity and synchronous composability in one state. In an ideal state, the fragmentation would not have happened, evidence of the base layers’ inherent weaknesses.LayerZero had to figure out the root causes of the fragmentation. Of the three forces that seem to have caused fragmentation—Technical Necessity, Capital Incentives, and Architectural Specialization—two of them were engineering problems solvable by a base layer with enough throughput and flexibility for specialized applications. The third force was financial incentives, which the market seems to have solved. The premium associated with launching a chain has collapsed in response to a plethora of L2 and app-chain tokens, as shown below. Investors no longer pay high multiples for similar applications wrapped in new tickers.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap as of June 11, 2026. For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security or cryptocurrency. Past performance is not indicative of future results.The financial incentives that once pushed teams toward fragmentation now are forcing consolidation. The other two forces are solvable engineering problems.Where Does LayerZero Go Next?Over the past five years, LayerZero has built the messaging infrastructure that connects 170+ blockchains, facilitated more than $270 billion in cumulative cross-chain value transfers, and achieved the institutional traction associated with running production infrastructure at scale. OFT has become the de facto standard for unified-supply tokens. Stargate was, at one point, one of the most significant cross-chain venues in the market. Just as important, across the L1 stack, the LayerZero team has developed depth of expertise that we believe few others, if any, in the industry can match.As with most startups, LayerZero’s track record has some blemishes. Earlier this year, the rsETH incident compelled LayerZero Labs to become more outspoken on security away from the protocol. The Lab now is refusing, for example, to interact with 1/1 DVN setups. While it did not invalidate LayerZero’s architecture, rsETH highlighted the importance of using the correct configuration of the architecture. That said, the team remains committed to enhancing its decentralized, permissionless, and censorship-resistant cross-chain layer.After five years of detailed and complicated work on cross-chain integration, LayerZero is convinced that if it were to rebuild each layer of the stack using first principles, addressing every bottleneck, the improvements would compound and produce performance gains orders of magnitude beyond any single breakthrough, without sacrificing the power of the technology.That conviction has become the inspiration and motivation for Zero: a Layer 1 that combines several breakthroughs into a unified system. In Part 2 of this series, we detail those breakthroughs and explain Zero’s novel architecture.Important InformationARK Investment Management LLC, and its affiliates, are investors in LayerZero Labs and the ZRO token, have entered into material agreements with LayerZero Labs, and have an incentive to promote LayerZero Labs and the ZRO Token. In the context of cryptocurrencies, a “primitive” is a foundational general purpose capability that does not solve one specific problem but acts as a building block to solve many. Applications and other protocols build on top of primitives to construct more complex systems.

3

“Perps” (perpetual futures) are derivatives contracts without an expiration date that allow traders to speculate on the underlying asset prices indefinitely.

4

Layer 1s are independent blockchain networks with their own consensus and security mechanisms. Layer 2s are blockchains that scale Layer 1s by executing transactions off the base layer while relying on the underlying Layer 1 for settlement and security.

5

Optimistic fraud proofs are a security mechanism that allows assets to be withdrawn or settled from an optimistic rollup to Ethereum only after a challenge period, typically seven days. During this period, anyone can contest an invalid state transition by submitting a fraud proof. If successful, the invalid state is rejected, ensuring that only correctly computed balances ultimately can be settled on Ethereum.
